notes.heading: What travels and what oscillates
paragraphs: A progressive wave transfers energy through a medium or field while a pattern propagates. In a simple wave on a string, each element oscillates about its equilibrium position; the element does not travel along the whole string with the pattern. Amplitude is the maximum magnitude of displacement, not the full peak-to-peak distance. Wavelength is a spatial repetition distance measured between neighbouring points in the same phase. Period is a temporal repetition interval at a fixed position.

In a transverse wave, displacement is perpendicular to the direction of propagation; in a longitudinal wave it is parallel. Sound in air is longitudinal, while an ideal wave on a stretched string is transverse. Electromagnetic waves involve oscillating fields and need no material medium. Polarisation restricts the direction of transverse oscillation and therefore supplies evidence for transverse behaviour. A longitudinal sound wave cannot be polarised in that same displacement-direction sense.

notes.heading: Connecting speed, frequency and graphs
paragraphs: A travelling pattern moves one wavelength during one period, so v=λ/T=fλ and f=1/T. Convert units before substitution: a period of 4 ms is 0.004 s, corresponding to 250 Hz. Frequency is measured in cycles per second, whereas angular phase is expressed in degrees or radians. Do not confuse the speed of the propagating wave with the instantaneous speed of an oscillating particle.

A displacement-position graph at one instant can reveal wavelength but not period without extra information. A displacement-time graph at one position reveals period but not wavelength on its own. Always read the horizontal-axis label before measuring a separation. When a source frequency changes in a medium where the relevant wave speed is approximately fixed, the wavelength adjusts inversely. That is an assumption about the medium and regime, not a rule that every possible wave speed is frequency independent.

notes.heading: Phase comparisons
paragraphs: For points along a sinusoidal progressive wave at the same instant, a separation Δx corresponds to phase magnitude 2πΔx/λ radians, or 360Δx/λ degrees. Phase differences differing by a whole number of cycles describe the same relative phase. A separation of one wavelength is therefore in phase; half a wavelength gives antiphase. Stating which point leads also requires the propagation direction and an agreed sign convention.

For observations at one position separated in time, use 2πΔt/T instead. Do not mix a time separation with wavelength. Phase is not the same as displacement: two points may have equal displacement while moving in opposite directions and therefore not be in phase. For a complete phase comparison, the state of oscillation includes both displacement and direction of motion.

notes.heading: Superposition creates stationary patterns
paragraphs: Within the linear approximation, overlapping wave displacements add algebraically. Two identical-frequency waves of equal amplitude travelling in opposite directions can produce a stationary pattern. At nodes the displacements cancel at every time; at antinodes the oscillation amplitude is largest. For an ideal equal-amplitude pair, an antinode reaches twice the amplitude of either contributing wave. That does not imply every point always has that displacement.

Adjacent nodes are separated by λ/2, and a node to the nearest antinode by λ/4, where λ is the wavelength of the contributing travelling waves. The pattern's nodes stay in place even though the constituent waves propagate. Points within one node-to-node loop oscillate in phase, while neighbouring loops oscillate in antiphase. The ideal stationary pattern carries no net time-averaged energy along the string; real driven systems still require input to offset dissipative losses.

notes.heading: Harmonics of a fixed-end string
paragraphs: If both ends of an ideal string are nodes, the length L contains an integer number n of half-wavelengths: L=nλ/2. Thus λn=2L/n and fn=nv/(2L). For tension F and mass per unit length μ, the ideal string speed is √(F/μ), giving f1=(1/(2L))√(F/μ). Use first harmonic for n=1 in the AQA terminology mapped here. The symbol for tension is sometimes T, so distinguish it from period when reading a formula.

Holding other variables fixed, doubling length halves the first-harmonic frequency, quadrupling tension doubles it, and quadrupling linear density halves it. These predictions depend on the ideal-string assumptions. In a supervised investigation, repeated measurements and a graph can test the predicted relationship; changing several factors at once obscures which caused a shift. Use the taught laboratory risk assessment for stretched wires, masses and apparatus. This text does not replace that assessment or demonstrate a student's practical competence.

notes.heading: Scope and revision sequence
paragraphs: The source crosswalk covers selected progressive-wave quantities, wave type/polarisation reasoning and stationary-string theory in AQA 7408. Full graphical construction of superposition, microwave and sound arrangements, and assessed practical skills still need additional resources. A correct calculation in this lesson does not complete the whole waves unit or certify a laboratory activity.

First identify the kind of graph or wave pattern, then choose the relation that connects the given quantities. Draw or describe the node arrangement before assigning a harmonic number. Check dimensions in the string formula: tension divided by linear density has units of speed squared. Finish with units and a statement of whether the result describes a constituent wave, the stationary pattern or an oscillating particle.

notes.heading: Distinguishing a harmonic number from adjacent nodes
paragraphs: A stationary wave on an ideal string fixed at both ends has nodes at the ends. Adjacent nodes are separated by half a wavelength, so the nth harmonic fits n half-wavelengths into the string length. Count intervals rather than just internal nodes. Once wavelength is found, use wave speed divided by wavelength for frequency. Increasing harmonic number at fixed length and speed increases frequency, while the distance between adjacent nodes decreases. The stationary pattern has fixed nodes and antinodes; it does not mean the string is motionless everywhere. The example assumes an ideal uniform string and fixed wave speed, rather than modelling tension changes or damping.

workedExamples.prompt: A wave has f=80 Hz and λ=0.45 m. Find its speed.
steps: Frequency times wavelength has units m/s.

workedExamples.prompt: Two points on a progressive wave are separated by 0.15 m, with wavelength 0.60 m. Find phase magnitude.
steps: The separation is one quarter of a wavelength.
No lead/lag sign is inferred without a direction convention.

workedExamples.prompt: A 0.90 m string fixed at both ends shows three loops. Wave speed is 120 m/s. Find frequency.
steps: Three loops give n=3 and λ=2L/n=0.60 m.
Check this is the third harmonic.

workedExamples.prompt: Tension is 64 N, linear density is 0.004 kg/m and length is 1 m. Find first-harmonic frequency.
steps: Round only after evaluating the square root.

workedExamples.prompt: A 1.5 m ideal string fixed at both ends vibrates in its third harmonic with wave speed 90 m s⁻¹. Find wavelength, frequency and adjacent-node spacing.
steps: Three half-wavelengths fill 1.5 m, so λ = 2L/3 = 1.0 m.
Adjacent nodes are λ/2 = 0.5 m apart.
workedExamples.answer: Wavelength 1.0 m; frequency 90 Hz; adjacent-node spacing 0.5 m.

misconceptions.claim: A node means no waves pass through that location.
misconceptions.correction: The contributing waves overlap there and their displacements cancel.

misconceptions.claim: The distance between adjacent nodes is one wavelength.
misconceptions.correction: It is half the wavelength of either contributing travelling wave.

misconceptions.claim: Frequency and wave speed are the same quantity.
misconceptions.correction: Frequency counts cycles per time; speed measures propagation distance per time.

Speed is 200×0.75.

questions.prompt: Explain why a displacement-time graph at one point cannot by itself provide wavelength.
questions.answer: It gives temporal repetition and thus period, but no spatial repetition distance. Wave speed or spatial data are also needed.
solution: Identify the time axis.
Distinguish temporal and spatial repetition.
markingPoints: Identify what can be measured.
State the missing information.

questions.prompt: A 1.2 m fixed-end string has wave speed 96 m/s. Find its second-harmonic frequency in Hz.
questions.answer: 80 Hz.
solution: Use f2=2v/(2L).
Calculate 96/1.2.
markingPoints: Use the second-harmonic relation.

questions.prompt: Distinguish a node from a point that happens to pass through equilibrium.
questions.answer: A node has zero amplitude throughout the oscillation. Other points pass through zero displacement at particular instants but usually have nonzero amplitude and velocity.
solution: Separate displacement at an instant from amplitude.
Describe persistent cancellation at a node.
Compare an ordinary oscillating point.
markingPoints: Define a node.
Distinguish instantaneous displacement.
Explain the ordinary equilibrium crossing.

questions.prompt: Two points are 0.20 m apart on a progressive wave of wavelength 0.80 m. Give the phase magnitude in degrees.
solution: The separation is 0.25 wavelength.
Multiply 0.25 by 360°.
markingPoints: Use the spatial fraction of a cycle.
Obtain 90°.

questions.prompt: Why should an experiment varying string tension keep vibrating length and linear density fixed?
questions.answer: The first-harmonic frequency depends on all three. Fixing the other two isolates the predicted dependence on tension; repeats and uncertainty estimates are still needed.
solution: Identify the variables in f1=(1/(2L))√(F/μ).
Explain the confounding effect of simultaneous changes.
State a further measurement-quality requirement.
markingPoints: Identify all relevant variables.
Explain control of variables.
Include repeatability or uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Why can a longitudinal sound wave in air not be polarised like a transverse string wave?
questions.answer: Its particle displacement is along the propagation direction, so there is no transverse displacement orientation to select.
solution: State the longitudinal displacement direction.
Contrast it with selectable transverse directions.
markingPoints: Describe longitudinal motion.
Explain the polarisation distinction.

questions.prompt: A 1.5 m ideal string fixed at both ends vibrates in its third harmonic with wave speed 90 m s⁻¹. Find wavelength, frequency and adjacent-node spacing.
questions.answer: Wavelength 1.0 m; frequency 90 Hz; adjacent-node spacing 0.5 m.
solution: Three half-wavelengths fill 1.5 m, so λ = 2L/3 = 1.0 m.
Frequency is v/λ = 90/1.0 = 90 Hz.
Adjacent nodes are λ/2 = 0.5 m apart.
markingPoints: Three half-wavelengths fill 1.5 m, so λ = 2L/3 = 1.0 m.
Frequency is v/λ = 90/1.0 = 90 Hz.
Adjacent nodes are λ/2 = 0.5 m apart.

questions.prompt: A learner counts two internal nodes and calls this the second harmonic. Explain the counting error and state the total number of nodes including both ends.
questions.answer: It is the third harmonic because there are three half-wavelength intervals. There are four nodes including the two ends.
solution: Both fixed ends are nodes in addition to the two internal nodes.
Four nodes delimit three adjacent intervals.
Each interval is half a wavelength, so three intervals identify harmonic number three.
markingPoints: Both fixed ends are nodes in addition to the two internal nodes.
Four nodes delimit three adjacent intervals.
Each interval is half a wavelength, so three intervals identify harmonic number three.
